name: Critical Thinking and Spotting Misinformation
objectives: When a post makes you feel strongly, pause and ask who made it, what the evidence is and what others say, before you believe or share it
Given a website or account, check who is behind it by reading what other trusted sources say about it, finding at least two other sources before you decide
Given a dramatic picture, run a reverse image search to find where and when it first appeared, writing down the oldest date you find and whether it matches the post

After checking a surprising post, write a short verdict with evidence and note how your own feelings or beliefs may have pulled you, in three sentences with a clear true, false, misleading or not sure yet

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Stop and check a claim
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pause before you believe or share, and ask three quick questions.
This lesson builds toward: When a post makes you feel strongly, you will pause and ask who made it, what the evidence is and what others say, before you believe or share it.
False posts spread fastest when they make us feel something strong: anger, fear, pride or excitement. That feeling is your signal to stop. A few seconds of checking can stop you from passing on something false to people who trust you.
Ask three questions. Who is behind this? (A real news outlet, a government office, a doctor, or an account you have never heard of?) What is the evidence? (A link to a study, a document, a video of the whole event, or just someone's say-so?) What do other trusted sources say? (Is anyone else reporting this?)
A useful set of steps is called SIFT: Stop; Investigate the source; Find better coverage; Trace claims, quotes and pictures back to where they first appeared. You will practise each part in this course. If you are not sure, it is fine to wait. Not sharing is always an option.
Step by step:
- Notice a strong feeling: that is your signal to stop.
- Ask: who is behind this?
- Ask: what is the evidence?
- Ask: what do other trusted sources say?
- Not sure? Do not share yet.
Words to know:
- Misinformation: false information shared by people who may think it is true.
- Disinformation: false information made and spread on purpose to fool people.
- Claim: something a post says is true.
Official sources:
- Digital Inquiry Group: Civic Online Reasoning (free lessons on evaluating online information)
Try it now: Open your social media, news app or a family group chat. Find one post that made you feel something strong. Write down the answers to the three questions: who, what evidence, what others say.
You can now pause when a post stirs strong feelings and ask who is behind it, what the evidence is and what others say.

check.q: Which question helps you check a claim?
options: How many likes does it have?
Who made this, and what is their evidence?
Is the picture colorful?
Did my friend share it?
check.why: Asking who made it and what evidence they have is part of stopping to check.

check.q: A family group chat forwards a shocking warning. What would you do first?
options: Forward it to everyone right away
Delete the group chat
Pause and check before you share
Reply in all capitals
check.why: Strong feelings are a signal to stop and check first.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Lateral reading: checking the source
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check who is behind a website or account by reading other sites about it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a website or account, you will check who is behind it by reading what other trusted sources say about it, finding at least two other sources before you decide.
Fake sites can look very professional, with logos, "About us" pages and official-sounding names. Reading the site itself will not tell you if you can trust it. Professional fact-checkers do something else: they leave the site and read sideways. This is called lateral reading.
Open a new tab and search for the name of the site, the organization or the person, plus words like "who funds" or "reliable". See what others say about them: news outlets, Wikipedia's article on them, or fact-checking sites such as AP Fact Check, Reuters Fact Check, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org or Snopes. A health claim? Check what your doctor or official health sites say. A claim about a government program? Go to the official site, often ending in .gov.
Also look for the same story from at least two trusted sources you already know. If only one unknown site is reporting something huge, be careful.
Step by step:
- Do not judge a site by its own looks or "About us" page.
- Open a new tab.
- Search the site, group or person's name plus "reliable" or "who funds".
- Read what news outlets, Wikipedia or fact-checkers say about them.
- Look for the same story from two trusted sources.
Words to know:
- Lateral reading: checking a source by leaving it and reading what other sites say about it.
- Fact-checker: a person or group whose job is to check if claims are true.
Official sources:
- Digital Inquiry Group: Intro to Lateral Reading (Civic Online Reasoning)
Try it now: Take the post from Lesson 1. Open a new tab and search for the name of the site or account that posted it. Write one sentence about what other sources say about it, and whether any trusted outlet reports the same story.
You can now check a website or account by reading what other trusted sources say about it.

options: Opening new tabs to see what other sources say about a site
Reading a page from top to bottom slowly
Reading only the headline
Reading the site's About us page
check.why: Lateral reading checks a source by leaving it and reading others about it.

check.q: You find a news site you have never heard of with a big story. What would you do?
options: Trust it because it looks professional
Share it so others can decide
Read only its About us page
Search the site's name and see what trusted sources say
check.why: What others say about a site tells you more than what it says about itself.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reverse image search: where did this picture come from?
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a reverse image search to find where a picture first appeared.
This lesson builds toward: Given a dramatic picture, you will run a reverse image search to find where and when it first appeared, writing down the oldest date you find and whether it matches the post.
Many false posts use a real photo with a false story: a flood picture from years ago shared as "today", or a photo from another country. A reverse image search finds where else a picture appears online, often showing its real date and story.
On a computer: go to google.com and click the camera icon ("Search by image"), then upload the picture or drag it into the search box. In the Chrome browser you can also right-click a picture on a website and choose "Search with Google Lens". On a phone, the Google app and Google Lens let you search with a picture or a screenshot. TinEye (tineye.com) is another free reverse image search site.
Look at the results for the oldest version, the place it first appeared, and news stories or fact-checks about it. If the picture is from a different time, place or event than the post says, the post is misleading even if the photo is real.
Step by step:
- Save or screenshot the picture.
- Open Google image search (camera icon) or Google Lens, or tineye.com.
- Upload the picture.
- Look for the oldest copy, where it first appeared, and any fact-checks.
- Compare: does the real story match what the post says?
Words to know:
- Reverse image search: searching with a picture to find where else it appears online.
- Screenshot: a picture of what is on your screen.
- Misleading: using something real in a way that gives a false idea.
Official sources:
- Google Search Help: Search with an image
Try it now: Find a dramatic photo in a post or news feed. Screenshot it and run a reverse image search. Write down the oldest date you can find and whether it matches the post's story.
You can now run a reverse image search and tell whether a real photo is being used with a false story.

check.q: What does a reverse image search use to search?
options: A word you type
A phone number
A voice recording
A picture
check.why: A reverse image search looks for other copies of a picture.

check.q: A reverse search shows a "today's storm" photo first appeared five years ago. What would you decide?
options: The post is misleading
The post is true
The photo is fake
Reverse search is broken
check.why: A real old photo shared as new is misleading.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: AI fakes, scams and your own mind

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Spotting deepfakes and AI fakes
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check a picture, video or voice that might be made by AI.
This lesson builds toward: Given a video, picture or voice that might be made by AI, you will check it against the person's official account and trusted news, and use a family code word for calls, without relying only on how it looks or sounds.
AI tools can now make pictures, videos and voices that look and sound real. A deepfake might show a famous person saying something they never said. A voice clone can copy a family member from a short clip of their voice.
Old tricks like counting fingers or looking for blurry ears still catch some fakes, but newer tools make fewer mistakes, so do not rely on looks alone. Check the context instead. Who posted it first? Is it on the person's or organization's real, official account? Do trusted news outlets report it? Some platforms and AI tools add labels or hidden marks to AI content, but many fakes have none, so a missing label does not prove something is real.
For calls and voice messages, the FTC's advice is simple: don't trust the voice. If a "grandchild" or "boss" calls asking for money or secrets, hang up and call them back at a number you already know. Some families agree on a code word for emergencies.
Step by step:
- Be extra careful with shocking videos, celebrity clips and urgent voice messages.
- Do not rely on looks alone.
- Check who posted it first and if it is on the real official account.
- Look for trusted news coverage.
- For voices: hang up and call back on a number you know.
Words to know:
- Deepfake: a fake video, picture or audio made with AI to look or sound like a real person.
- Voice clone: an AI copy of someone's voice.
- AI-generated: made by an AI tool rather than recorded from real life.
Official sources:
- FTC consumer alert: Scammers use AI to enhance their family emergency schemes
Try it now: Find a viral video or picture of a famous person. Check who posted it first, whether it appears on that person's official account, and whether trusted news outlets mention it. Then agree a family code word with someone you love.
You can now check a possible AI fake by its context and protect yourself from cloned voices.

check.q: What is a family code word for?
options: Logging in to your bank
Checking that a caller really is your family member
Joining a group chat
Making AI voices
check.why: A code word helps you check a caller when a voice could be faked.

check.q: A video shows a famous person saying something shocking. What would you do?
options: Share it because it looks real
Decide by looking closely at the face
Assume it is fake and share that
Check their official account and trusted news first
check.why: Check the source and trusted coverage; looks alone are not enough.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Scams that use fake news
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot fake news stories and ads that are really scams.
This lesson builds toward: Given an ad or post that promises money, a cure or a big deal, you will list the scam warning signs and report it, finding every warning sign before you click, pay or sign up.
Many scams dress up as news. A fake article shows a famous person "revealing" a get-rich-quick investment, a miracle cure or a free government payment, with a link to sign up. Fake charity appeals appear right after disasters. Fake ads on social media promise huge "limited time" discounts. Some fake stories use AI-made video of celebrities or news anchors.
Warning signs: it rushes you; it promises big money, a cure or a prize; it asks you to pay with gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency; it asks for passwords, codes or ID numbers; or the link goes to a website that is not the real one. The FTC says only scammers tell you to buy a gift card to pay them.
What to do: do not click the link. Go to the real organization's website by typing its address yourself, or call a number you already know. Give to charities you can look up. If you or a loved one lost money, contact your bank right away, and report the scam to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov (in the US).
Step by step:
- Watch for news-style posts that sell something or ask for money.
- Look for warning signs: rush, big promises, gift cards, wire or crypto, codes.
- Do not click the link.
- Type the real website yourself or call a number you know.
- Lost money? Call your bank, then report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Words to know:
- Scam: a trick to steal money or information.
- Phishing: fake messages that try to get you to click a link or share private details.
- Sponsored post: a paid ad on social media; it may not be checked.
Official sources:
- FTC: Avoiding and reporting gift card scams
- FTC: Government and business impersonators
- FTC: ReportFraud
Try it now: Look through your social media or messages for one ad or post that promises money, a cure or a big discount. List every warning sign you can see. If it is a scam, use the platform's menu to report it.
You can now spot scams that look like news, avoid their links and know where to report them.

check.q: Which is a sign that a post is a scam?
options: It asks you to pay with gift cards
It links to a real .gov address you typed yourself
It gives time to think
It comes from a charity you know and trust
check.why: Requests for gift card payments are a clear scam sign.

check.q: An ad says a famous doctor found a miracle cure and you must buy today. What would you do?
options: Buy it before it sells out
Share it with sick friends
Check with your doctor or official health sources and report the ad
Give your card number to learn more
check.why: Health claims go to a doctor or official source, and scams should be reported.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Bias in your own thinking
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Notice when your own beliefs or feelings are steering what you accept as true.
This lesson builds toward: After checking a surprising post, you will write a short verdict with evidence and note how your own feelings or beliefs may have pulled you, in three sentences with a clear true, false, misleading or not sure yet.
The hardest fakes to catch are the ones we want to believe. Confirmation bias means we quickly accept things that fit what we already think and look hard for problems in things that do not. Everyone does it, whatever their age, background or politics.
Social media can make it stronger. Feeds show us more of what we already click on, so we can end up seeing only one side. A post shared by a friend feels trustworthy, but your friend may not have checked it either.
Three habits help. Ask: "Would I believe this if it were about the other side?" Ask: "What evidence would change my mind?" And go looking for a trusted source that might disagree. Changing your mind when the facts change is a strength, not a weakness. Before you share, take one last look: is it true, is it helpful, and is it fair?
Step by step:
- Notice when a post feels "just right" for what you already think.
- Ask: would I believe this if it were about the other side?
- Ask: what evidence would change my mind?
- Look for a trusted source that might disagree.
- Before sharing: is it true, helpful and fair?
Words to know:
- Bias: a leaning that can push our thinking one way without us noticing.
- Confirmation bias: accepting what fits our beliefs and doubting what does not.
- Echo chamber: a place where you only hear views that match your own.
Try it now: Final task: take one surprising post and check it with every step in this course. Write a three-sentence verdict (true, false, misleading or not sure yet) with your evidence, and note one way your own feelings might have pulled you.
You can now check a post from start to finish and notice when your own bias is pulling you.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Paused and asked Shared or believed it without checking. Wrote who made it, the evidence and what others say. Noted the feeling that made them want to share. Source checked Relied on the site's own page or the post alone. Read what at least two other sources say about the site or account. Found the story, or its absence, in trusted outlets and fact-checkers. Picture traced No reverse image search on a picture in the post. Ran a reverse image search and wrote the oldest date found. Explained whether the picture matches the post's time and place. Scam signs Missed clear scam signs such as pressure or gift-card payment. Listed every scam sign, or confirmed there were none. Reported it on the platform if it was a scam. Verdict and bias No clear verdict, or no evidence given. A three-sentence verdict with evidence and a decision about sharing. Also notes how their own feelings or beliefs may have pulled them. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: A place where you only hear views like your own
A room with loud sound
A fact-checking website
A type of AI tool
check.why: In an echo chamber you mostly hear what you already think.

check.q: A post about a politician you dislike makes you happy and you want to share it. What would you do?
options: Share it because it fits what you think
Share it with a joke
Ask if you would believe it about the other side, and check it
Ignore all news from now on
check.why: Asking that question helps catch your own bias before you share.
